questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java?
questions.title: Functional Interface in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have multiple default and static methods. The @FunctionalInterface annotation verifies this at compile time. Functional interfaces are the target type for lambda expressions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Foundational Java 8 knowledge — functional interfaces are the contract for lambdas
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @FunctionalInterface creates the constraint — the annotation only validates it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the four key built-in functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier

sections.title: What Makes an Interface Functional
sections.content:
A **functional interface** is any interface with exactly one abstract method. This single abstract method (SAM) is the key — it's what allows Java to convert a lambda expression into an implementation of that interface.

Think of it like a contract with one specific job: the lambda provides the implementation for that one method, and Java handles the rest. The interface can have as many **default methods** (with bodies) and **static methods** as you want — those don't count toward the SAM rule. The **@FunctionalInterface** annotation is optional but recommended: it tells the compiler to enforce the one-abstract-method rule, preventing you from accidentally adding a second abstract method later. Without functional interfaces, lambdas wouldn't have a type to target. They're the bridge between Java's object-oriented type system and the functional programming style introduced in Java 8.

> **The gotcha:** `@FunctionalInterface` doesn't *create* the rule — any interface with one abstract method already works as a lambda target, exactly like `Runnable` always has.

sections.title: Functional Interface at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Functional interface|~exactly one abstract method|the SAM|target type for a lambda|@FunctionalInterface optional
blue|Allowed extras|~default methods OK|static methods OK|Object methods don't count|equals / hashCode / toString
emerald|Examples|~Runnable, Callable|Comparator, Predicate|Function, Supplier|your own custom SAM

sections.title: Custom Functional Interface with Lambda Usage
When to Use Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
Use functional interfaces when you need to **pass behavior as a parameter** — like validation logic to a filter method, or a transformation rule to a mapper. They're essential for **Stream API operations** where you pass lambdas to filter(), map(), or forEach(). Create **custom functional interfaces** when the built-in ones (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier) don't match your method signature — for example, if you need a method that takes three parameters or throws checked exceptions.

Use them in **event handling** where a listener needs to react to domain events. They're the foundation for making your code more flexible and testable by treating operations as first-class values.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding a second abstract method**: Freshers often add another abstract method to an interface marked @FunctionalInterface, breaking the SAM rule. The compiler catches this if you use the annotation, but without it you'll get cryptic lambda compilation errors.
- **Confusing default methods with abstract methods**: Default methods have implementations (the default keyword) so they don't count toward the one-abstract-method limit. Freshers sometimes think any method in the interface breaks the functional interface rule.
- **Forgetting the annotation**: While @FunctionalInterface is optional, skipping it means you won't get a compile-time error if someone later adds a second abstract method, breaking all the lambdas that use your interface.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single Abstract Method (SAM)**: exactly one abstract method defines the functional interface contract
- **@FunctionalInterface**: optional annotation that enforces the SAM rule at compile time
- **Default and static methods**: allowed in unlimited quantity — they don't count as abstract methods
- **Lambda target type**: functional interfaces are what lambdas compile to — the lambda implements the single abstract method
- **Built-in interfaces**: Java provides Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier for common patterns
- **Method references**: functional interfaces enable :: syntax like String::toLowerCase
- **Pre-Java 8 examples**: Runnable and Callable were functional interfaces before the term existed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. That's the key rule. The single abstract method is what allows you to use a lambda expression as an implementation of that interface. So when you write something like orders.filter with a lambda that takes an order and returns a boolean, that lambda is implementing a functional interface — in this case, Predicate. Now, the interface can also have default methods and static methods, as many as you want. Those don't count toward the rule because they already have implementations. The at-FunctionalInterface annotation is optional, but it's a good practice. It tells the compiler to check that you really do have exactly one abstract method. If you accidentally add a second one later, you'll get a compile error instead of breaking all your lambdas. Java provides four main built-in functional interfaces: Predicate for testing, Function for transforming, Consumer for side effects, and Supplier for producing values. But you can create your own when those don't fit. One mistake freshers make is thinking the annotation is required. It's not. Any interface with one abstract method works. Runnable is a functional interface and it doesn't have the annotation. The annotation just helps catch mistakes early.

questions.question: What is the difference between Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier?
questions.title: Predicate vs Function vs Consumer vs Supplier
questions.direct_answer: Predicate takes T and returns boolean for testing. Function takes T and returns R for transformation. Consumer takes T and returns nothing for side effects. Supplier takes nothing and returns T for production. These four patterns cover the fundamental operations: test, transform, act, and produce.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can name and distinguish the four key functional interfaces
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Function and Consumer — Function returns something, Consumer does not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete real-world use case for each from Stream operations

sections.title: The Four Core Functional Interface Patterns
sections.content:
Java 8 provides four fundamental functional interfaces that cover nearly every operation you'll need. **Predicate** tests a condition — it takes an input and returns true or false, perfect for filtering. **Function** transforms data — it takes one type and returns another, like converting a string to its length. **Consumer** performs side effects — it takes an input and returns nothing, used when you want to do something with a value (like printing or saving to a database). **Supplier** produces values — it takes no input and returns something, useful for lazy initialization or factory patterns. These aren't random choices — they map to the four things you can do with data: test it, transform it, act on it, or create it.

Understanding these four makes Stream API operations intuitive because almost every stream method uses one of them.

> **The gotcha:** the pair freshers mix up is `Function` versus `Consumer` — `Function` returns a value so the pipeline keeps flowing, while `Consumer` returns nothing and ends it.

sections.title: The Four Core Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
amber|Predicate<T>|~test(T) -> boolean|filtering conditions|and / or / negate|stream filter
blue|Function<T,R>|~apply(T) -> R|transform / map|andThen / compose|stream map
emerald|Consumer<T>|~accept(T) -> void|side effects|andThen chain|forEach
violet|Supplier<T>|~get() -> T|lazy value / factory|takes no input|orElseGet

sections.title: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier in code
Four Core Functional Interfaces Compared
sections.content:
| Interface | Signature | Purpose | Stream Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Predicate<T> | T → boolean | Test/filter data | filter(order -> order.amount() > 100) |
| Function<T,R> | T → R | Transform data | map(user -> user.email()) |
| Consumer<T> | T → void | Perform side effect | forEach(order -> logger.info(order)) |
| Supplier<T> | () → T | Produce/create data | generate(() -> UUID.randomUUID()) |

sections.title: When to Use Each Interface
sections.content:
Use **Predicate** when you need to filter or validate — deciding which elements to keep in a collection or whether an input meets criteria.

Use **Function** when you need to transform data types or extract properties — like mapping User objects to their email addresses or converting strings to integers.

Use **Consumer** when you need to perform actions without returning anything — logging, saving to a database, sending notifications, or updating UI.

Use **Supplier** when you need lazy initialization — deferring expensive object creation until actually needed, or providing default values in Optional.orElseGet(). In the Stream API: filter() takes Predicate, map() takes Function, forEach() takes Consumer, and generate() takes Supplier.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using Function when Consumer is correct**: Freshers often write lambdas that ignore the return value or return null, when they should use Consumer. If you're not returning anything meaningful, you need Consumer not Function.
- **Confusing input/output patterns**: Mixing up which interface takes what — especially confusing Supplier (no input) with Consumer (no output). The names help: Supplier supplies something, Consumer consumes something.
- **Not using method references**: Writing user -> user.getName() instead of User::getName when a simple method reference works. While both compile, the method reference is cleaner and shows you understand the connection between functional interfaces and existing methods.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Predicate<T>**: test() method returns boolean — used for filtering and validation logic
- **Function<T,R>**: apply() method transforms T to R — used for mapping and data transformation
- **Consumer<T>**: accept() method returns void — used for side effects like logging or persistence
- **Supplier<T>**: get() method produces T — used for lazy initialization and factory patterns
- **BiFunction and BiPredicate**: two-argument versions exist for operations needing two inputs
- **Primitive specializations**: IntPredicate, LongFunction avoid boxing for primitive types
- **Method composition**: these interfaces have default methods like and(), andThen(), compose() for chaining

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These four interfaces represent the four things you can do with data. Predicate is for testing — it takes an input and returns true or false. You use it in filter operations, like filtering orders where the amount is greater than a hundred. Function is for transformation — it takes one type and returns another type. You use it in map operations, like mapping a User to their email address. Consumer is for side effects — it takes an input but returns nothing. You use it when you want to do something with each element, like logging it or saving it to a database. That's forEach. Supplier is for producing values — it takes no input and returns something. You use it for lazy initialization, like generating UUIDs only when needed. The key difference freshers miss is between Function and Consumer. Function returns something, Consumer doesn't. If you're not using the return value, you probably need Consumer not Function. In the Stream API, you'll see these everywhere: filter uses Predicate, map uses Function, forEach uses Consumer, and generate uses Supplier. Understanding these four makes the entire Streams API make sense.

questions.question: What is @FunctionalInterface annotation and is it required?
questions.title: @FunctionalInterface Annotation in Java
questions.direct_answer: @FunctionalInterface is an optional annotation that tells the compiler to verify the interface has exactly one abstract method. It is NOT required — any interface with one abstract method can be used as a functional interface. The annotation just prevents accidental addition of a second abstract method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that @FunctionalInterface is optional but recommended
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an interface MUST have @FunctionalInterface to be used as a lambda target
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Runnable and Callable work as functional interfaces without @FunctionalInterface on them

sections.title: The Optional Safety Net for Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
The **@FunctionalInterface** annotation is a compiler directive that validates an interface follows the functional interface contract — exactly one abstract method.

Think of it like @Override: it doesn't change what your code does, but it prevents mistakes. If you mark an interface with @FunctionalInterface and then add a second abstract method, the compiler immediately stops you with an error. Without the annotation, the interface would silently stop being a functional interface, and all your lambda expressions using it would break with confusing errors. The annotation is **completely optional** — Runnable, Callable, and Comparator are all functional interfaces but were created before Java 8, so they don't have the annotation. Any interface with exactly one abstract method can be used as a lambda target, annotated or not. The annotation is documentation and validation, not a requirement.

> **The gotcha:** `@FunctionalInterface` is never required — `Runnable` and `Callable` work as lambda targets without it; the annotation only validates the single-abstract-method rule.

sections.title: @FunctionalInterface at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@FunctionalInterface|~compiler safety check|fails if 0 or 2+ abstract methods|documents intent|optional, not required
blue|Works without it|~lambda still compiles|the annotation only guards|protects against future edits|self-documenting
emerald|Doesn't count|~default methods|static methods|public Object methods|only the abstract SAM matters

sections.title: Functional Interface With and Without Annotation
When to Use @FunctionalInterface
sections.content:
Use @FunctionalInterface when you're **designing an interface explicitly for lambda usage** — it signals your intent to other developers and catches mistakes early. Always use it for **custom functional interfaces in your codebase** where maintainability matters — if someone adds a second abstract method six months later, the compiler will catch it immediately instead of breaking all the call sites.

Use it for **API design** where you're providing interfaces for clients to implement with lambdas — the annotation makes the contract explicit. Skip it only for **legacy interfaces** that happen to be functional but weren't designed as such. The annotation is especially valuable in **team environments** where multiple developers modify interfaces — it's a guard rail that prevents accidental breaking changes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking it's required**: Freshers often believe an interface won't work with lambdas unless it has @FunctionalInterface. They'll see Runnable.run() used with lambdas and wonder why it works without the annotation. The annotation is validation, not a requirement.
- **Adding it to interfaces with multiple abstract methods**: Some freshers annotate every interface with @FunctionalInterface, then get confused by compiler errors. If your interface naturally needs two abstract methods, it's not functional and shouldn't be annotated.
- **Forgetting default methods don't count**: Freshers sometimes hesitate to add a default method to a @FunctionalInterface, thinking it will break the annotation. Default methods have implementations, so they don't count toward the one-abstract-method rule.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Optional annotation**: any interface with one abstract method is functional, with or without the annotation
- **Compile-time validation**: the annotation makes the compiler enforce the single-abstract-method rule
- **Intent documentation**: it signals to developers that this interface is designed for lambda usage
- **Legacy interfaces**: Runnable and Callable are functional interfaces without the annotation
- **Default methods allowed**: you can add as many default methods as needed without breaking the annotation
- **Static methods allowed**: static methods in the interface also don't count toward the abstract method limit
- **Best practice**: always use @FunctionalInterface for custom interfaces designed for lambdas

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The at-FunctionalInterface annotation is optional. That's the most important thing to understand. Any interface with exactly one abstract method can be used as a functional interface, whether you annotate it or not. So what does the annotation do? It tells the compiler to check that your interface really does have exactly one abstract method. If you mark an interface with at-FunctionalInterface and then accidentally add a second abstract method, the compiler will give you an error immediately. Without the annotation, the interface would just silently stop being functional, and you'd get confusing errors where you try to use lambdas with it. Think of it like at-Override. It doesn't change how your code works, but it catches mistakes. Runnable is a great example. It's been a functional interface since Java 1.0, long before the annotation existed. It has one abstract method, run, so you can use it with lambdas even though it doesn't have the annotation. The same with Callable. Should you use the annotation? Yes, for custom interfaces you're designing for lambdas. It makes your intent clear and prevents future mistakes. But don't think it's required. It's a safety net, not a requirement.

questions.question: How do you compose two Predicates in Java 8?
questions.title: Composing Predicates in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: Predicate has default methods and(), or(), and negate() for composition. p1.and(p2) creates a new Predicate that is true only when both are true. p1.or(p2) is true when either is true. p.negate() inverts the Predicate. These compose predicates without nesting lambdas.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java 8 Predicate composition — shows real usage beyond just definitions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using && inside a lambda instead of and() method — works but misses the composition approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how composed predicates make stream filters more readable and reusable

sections.title: Building Complex Filters Through Composition
sections.content:
**Predicate composition** lets you build complex filtering logic from simple, reusable pieces. Instead of writing one giant lambda with nested conditions, you create small predicates and combine them with **and()**, **or()**, and **negate()** methods.

Think of it like building with LEGO blocks: each predicate is a single block testing one condition, and composition methods snap them together. The and() method creates a new predicate that's true only when both predicates are true (logical AND). The or() method creates one that's true when either is true (logical OR). The negate() method inverts a predicate, turning true to false and vice versa. The power is in **reusability** — you can define predicates once and combine them in different ways across your codebase. This makes filters more readable, testable, and maintainable than inline lambdas with complex boolean expressions.

> **The gotcha:** `and()` and `or()` return a *new* `Predicate` — they never mutate the original, so you have to use the value they hand back.

sections.title: Composing Predicates
sections.content:
amber|and()|~both must be true|short-circuits|p1.and(p2)|AND logic
blue|or()|~either may be true|short-circuits|p1.or(p2)|OR logic
emerald|negate()|~flips the result|p.negate()|NOT logic|reuse a condition

sections.title: Composing Predicates for Order Filtering
When to Use Predicate Composition
sections.content:
Use composition when you have **multiple filtering conditions that vary across use cases** — like filtering orders by status, amount, and customer type where different screens need different combinations.

Use it to **avoid duplicating complex logic** — define each condition once as a named predicate, then compose them instead of copying the same lambda everywhere.

Use it for **building dynamic filters** where users select which conditions to apply — you can conditionally add predicates based on user input.

Use it to make **stream filters more readable** — filter(isHighValue.and(isPending)) is clearer than filter(o -> o.amount() > 1000 && "PENDING".equals(o.status())).

Use composition when **testing filters** — you can unit-test each predicate independently, then trust that composition works correctly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using boolean operators instead of methods**: Freshers write order -> isHighValue(order) && isPending(order) inside a lambda instead of using isHighValue.and(isPending). Both work, but the method-based approach allows reusing composed predicates.
- **Not extracting reusable predicates**: Freshers inline all logic in stream filters, repeating the same conditions. Extract conditions into named predicates so you can reuse and compose them.
- **Confusing and() with logical AND**: The and() method returns a NEW predicate — it doesn't modify the existing one. Freshers sometimes think isHighValue.and(isPending) changes isHighValue. It doesn't. You must use the returned composed predicate.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **and() method**: returns a new Predicate that is true only when both predicates are true
- **or() method**: returns a new Predicate that is true when either predicate is true
- **negate() method**: returns a new Predicate that inverts the boolean result
- **Immutable composition**: composition methods return new predicates without modifying originals
- **Reusability**: define predicates once and compose them in multiple filters
- **Readability**: composed predicates with names are clearer than complex lambda expressions
- **Testability**: you can unit-test individual predicates before composing them

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You compose predicates using three methods: and, or, and negate. Let's say you have two predicates. One checks if an order amount is over a thousand. Another checks if the status is pending. If you want a predicate that's true only when both conditions are met, you use the and method. So isHighValue.and(isPending) gives you a new predicate that returns true only when the order is high value AND pending. The or method works the same way but for either-or logic. If you want to invert a predicate, use negate. So isPending.negate() gives you a predicate for non-pending orders. The key thing is these methods return a NEW predicate. They don't modify the original ones. Why is this better than just using double ampersand inside a lambda? Because you can define each condition once as a named predicate and reuse it across your codebase. Instead of copying the same lambda logic everywhere, you compose predicates. It makes your stream filters way more readable. Instead of filter with a giant lambda full of boolean logic, you write filter with a composed predicate that has a meaningful name. And you can test each predicate independently. Common mistake: freshers write the boolean logic inside lambdas instead of using composition. It works, but you miss the reusability.

questions.question: What is Function.andThen() vs Function.compose() in Java?
questions.title: Function.andThen() vs Function.compose()
questions.direct_answer: f.andThen(g) means apply f first, then apply g to the result (left to right: f then g). f.compose(g) means apply g first, then apply f to the result (right to left: g then f). andThen is more intuitive for sequential thinking.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Function composition methods — shows depth of Java 8 knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting the order backwards for compose()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show with types: f: A→B, g: B→C, f.andThen(g) gives A→C

sections.title: Two Directions for Function Composition
sections.content:
Function composition lets you chain transformations, but Java gives you two ways to think about the order: **andThen()** and **compose()**.

The difference is which function runs first. With **andThen()**, you're saying "do this function, THEN do that function" — it reads left to right, matching how you naturally think about sequences. If f converts a string to uppercase and g counts the length, then f.andThen(g) first uppercases, then counts. With **compose()**, you're thinking backwards — if you have a function f that operates on type B, and you compose it with g that produces B from A, the result is a function from A to whatever f produces. It's right-to-left: apply g first to get B, then apply f. Most developers prefer andThen because it matches sequential thinking, but compose is useful when you're building pipelines where you want to specify the final transformation first.

> **The gotcha:** `f.compose(g)` runs `g` first, not `f` — the object you call it on runs *second*, which is the exact reverse of `andThen`.

sections.title: andThen vs compose
sections.content:
amber|andThen(g)|~this first, then g|f.andThen(g) = g(f(x))|left to right|reads naturally
blue|compose(g)|~g first, then this|f.compose(g) = f(g(x))|right to left|pre-process the input
emerald|Tip|~same result, order differs|pick by readability|chain multiple andThen|each returns a new Function

sections.title: andThen vs compose, same functions
andThen vs compose
sections.content:
| Aspect | andThen() | compose() |
|---|---|---|
| Execution order | f.andThen(g): f first, g second | f.compose(g): g first, f second |
| Reading direction | Left to right (f → g) | Right to left (g → f) |
| Mental model | Do f, THEN do g | Before f, do g |
| Type flow | A → B (f), B → C (g), result: A → C | B → C (f), A → B (g), result: A → C |
| Common usage | Sequential pipeline building | Wrapping with preprocessing |

sections.title: When to Use Each Composition Method
sections.content:
Use **andThen()** when you're building a **sequential transformation pipeline** where each step naturally follows the previous one — like validating input, then transforming it, then formatting the result. It's the intuitive choice for most scenarios because it reads like English: "do this, then do that." Use **compose()** when you're **adding preprocessing to an existing function** — if you have a function that operates on cleaned data, compose it with a sanitization function so the cleaning happens automatically before the main logic.

Use compose when you're thinking about **what needs to happen before** the current function runs. In practice, andThen is more commonly used because left-to-right thinking is more natural for sequential transformations, but compose is useful in functional programming patterns where you build complex functions by wrapping simpler ones.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Getting compose order backwards**: Freshers see f.compose(g) and think f runs first because it's the object. But g runs first — compose means "before doing f, do g." This backwards thinking is the most common source of bugs.
- **Using compose when andThen is clearer**: Freshers sometimes use compose trying to seem advanced, but it makes the code harder to read. If you're thinking sequentially, use andThen.
- **Not understanding the type constraints**: With f.andThen(g), the output type of f must match the input type of g. Freshers sometimes try to chain incompatible functions and get confused by the compiler errors.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **andThen(g)**: applies this function first, then applies g to the result — left to right execution
- **compose(g)**: applies g first, then applies this function to the result — right to left execution
- **Type matching**: for f.andThen(g), f's return type must match g's parameter type
- **Immutability**: both methods return a NEW function without modifying the original functions
- **Chaining**: you can chain multiple compositions like f.andThen(g).andThen(h)
- **Left-to-right preference**: andThen is more intuitive for most developers and most use cases
- **Mathematical notation**: compose matches mathematical function composition notation f∘g means f(g(x))

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference is which function runs first. With andThen, you apply the first function, THEN apply the second to the result. With compose, you apply the second function first, then apply the first to that result. It's about reading direction. Let me give you a concrete example. Say you have a function that trims whitespace from a string, and another that converts to uppercase. If you do trim.andThen(toUpperCase), it trims first, then uppercases the trimmed result. That's left to right — do trim, then do uppercase. If you do toUpperCase.compose(trim), trim runs first, then the result gets uppercased. That's right to left — before uppercasing, trim. Most people prefer andThen because it matches how you think about sequences: do this, then do that. Compose is useful when you're thinking about prerequisites — like what needs to happen before the main function runs. The types matter too. For trim.andThen(toUpperCase), trim returns a string and toUpperCase takes a string, so the types line up. If they don't match, it won't compile. Common mistake: freshers think the object in f.compose(g) runs first. It doesn't. The parameter g runs first. That's what compose means — before doing f, compose it with g.

questions.question: How do you create a custom functional interface in Java?
questions.title: Custom Functional Interface in Java
questions.direct_answer: Define an interface with exactly one abstract method and annotate it with @FunctionalInterface. Choose the method signature to match what your lambda will do. Custom functional interfaces are needed when none of the built-in ones (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier) match your signature.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to create reusable functional interfaces for domain-specific operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a custom functional interface when Function<T,R> or BiFunction would already work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a practical example: a functional interface that throws checked exceptions

sections.title: When Built-In Interfaces Aren't Enough
sections.content:
Creating a **custom functional interface** is straightforward: define an interface with exactly one abstract method, and annotate it with **@FunctionalInterface** for compile-time validation.

The key decision is choosing the right **method signature** — the parameter types and return type should match exactly what your domain operation needs. While Java provides Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier for common patterns, you need a custom interface when you have **domain-specific requirements** that don't fit those four: multiple parameters (more than two), **checked exceptions** in the signature, or a **semantically meaningful name** that makes your code self-documenting. For example, a PaymentProcessor is clearer than Function<Payment, Receipt> — the custom interface makes the intent explicit. Custom functional interfaces also let you add **default methods** for composition logic specific to your domain.

> **The gotcha:** skip the custom interface when a built-in fits — if your method takes one value and returns another, that's already `Function`, and reusing it beats reinventing `Predicate`.

sections.title: Custom Functional Interface with Checked Exceptions
When to Create Custom Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
Create a custom functional interface when you need **checked exceptions in the signature** — the built-in interfaces don't throw checked exceptions, so if your operation can throw IOException or SQLException, you need a custom interface. Create one when you need **more than two parameters** — BiFunction handles two, but if your operation needs three or more inputs, a custom interface is required. Create one for **domain clarity** — OrderProcessor.process(Order) is more self-documenting than Function<Order,Receipt>.

Use a custom interface when you want **domain-specific default methods** for composition — like a custom combinator method that makes sense for your business logic. Create one when you're designing a **callback API** where the name matters for understanding what the callback does — like EventListener or NotificationHandler.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Creating custom interfaces unnecessarily**: Freshers create a custom interface when Function<Order,String> would work fine. If the built-in interfaces fit, use them — they're well-known and integrate seamlessly with Stream API. Custom interfaces should add value, not just wrap existing patterns.
- **Not using @FunctionalInterface**: Freshers skip the annotation thinking it's optional. While technically true, without it you won't get compile-time enforcement. Someone can accidentally add a second abstract method later, breaking all lambdas.
- **Poor naming**: Naming your interface Processor or Handler is too generic. The name should clearly communicate what the operation does — OrderValidator is better than Validator, EmailSender is better than Sender.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single abstract method**: the core requirement — define exactly one abstract method with your needed signature
- **@FunctionalInterface annotation**: always use it for custom interfaces to get compile-time validation
- **Checked exceptions**: custom interfaces let you declare checked exceptions in the method signature
- **Multiple parameters**: use custom interfaces when you need more than two parameters (BiFunction limit)
- **Domain semantics**: custom names like OrderProcessor make code more self-documenting than generic Function
- **Default methods**: add domain-specific composition or utility methods as defaults
- **Fallback to built-ins**: if Predicate, Function, Consumer, or Supplier fit, use them instead of custom

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Creating a custom functional interface is simple. You define an interface with exactly one abstract method, and you annotate it with at-FunctionalInterface. The method signature should match what your operation needs — the parameter types and return type. When should you create a custom one instead of using the built-in ones? First, when you need checked exceptions. The standard functional interfaces like Function and Predicate don't declare checked exceptions. So if your operation can throw IOException or SQLException, you need a custom interface with throws in the signature. Second, when you need more than two parameters. Function takes one, BiFunction takes two. If you need three or more, you need a custom interface. Third, for domain clarity. Writing OrderProcessor.process is way clearer than Function apply. The custom name makes your code self-documenting. You can also add default methods to your custom interface for domain-specific composition logic. Like a custom combiner method that makes sense for your business rules. Common mistake: creating custom interfaces when the built-ins would work. If your operation takes one input and returns a result, that's Function. Don't create a custom interface just to wrap it. Use custom interfaces when they add real value — checked exceptions, multiple params, or meaningful names.
